notes.meaning: Jehoahaz son of Jehu becomes king over Israel in the city of Samaria while Joash is king in Judah. He rules for seventeen years. His reign begins the fulfillment of God's promise that Jehu's family would sit on Israel's throne for four generations.

Jehoahaz lives an ungodly life and repeats the sins of Jeroboam, who had set up golden calf idols at Bethel and Dan. Instead of leading the nation back to the true worship of God, he keeps this counterfeit state religion going.

Because of Israel's persistent idolatry, the Lord is angry and allows King Hazael of Aram and his son Ben-hadad to defeat them repeatedly. God uses these foreign enemies as a tool of discipline against His stubborn people.
In desperate trouble, Jehoahaz begs the Lord for help. Even though the king had not truly abandoned his sinful ways, God listens to his cry because He sees how cruelly Aram is crushing Israel.

God answers by providing a rescuer who frees Israel from the control of Aram, allowing the people to live safely in their homes once again. In the traditional view, this rescuer refers to King Jehoash and his son Jeroboam II, whom God used to win back Israel's lost cities.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars suggest the rescuer was King Adad-nirari III of Assyria, whose military strikes against Damascus broke Aram's power over Israel.

notes.meaning: Even after God shows mercy, the king and the people do not turn away from Jeroboam's false worship. They even leave an Asherah pole—a wooden idol used in Canaanite fertility worship—standing undisturbed in the capital city of Samaria.

Aram's brutal attacks leave Israel's army almost completely destroyed, reduced to only fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers. The enemy crushes them like grain trampled into fine dust on a threshing floor.

The writer directs the reader to the official royal records for the rest of Jehoahaz's deeds, including his personal courage in battle. His bravery shows that Israel's military collapse was not caused by a cowardly king, but by God's righteous judgment against the nation's sins.
Jehoahaz dies and is buried in Samaria alongside the earlier kings of Israel. His son Jehoash then takes the throne in his place.
Jehoash begins his sixteen-year reign over the northern kingdom of Israel while Joash rules over Judah. He rules from the capital city of Samaria during a troubled and violent era.

Jehoash continues the sinful pattern of the kings before him by keeping the worship of Jeroboam's golden calves. Despite seeing God's past judgments on the nation, he refuses to lead his people back to the Lord.

The writer notes that the rest of Jehoash's acts and military exploits, including his war against King Amaziah of Judah, are preserved in Israel's royal records. That war resulted in the defeat of Judah and serious damage to Jerusalem's walls.
Jehoash dies and is laid to rest in Samaria with the earlier kings of Israel. His son Jeroboam II succeeds him on the throne.

When the elderly prophet Elisha becomes deathly ill, King Jehoash visits him and weeps at his bedside. The king cries out that Elisha is the true chariot and horsemen of Israel, recognizing that the prophet's prayers and spiritual guidance were the nation's real defense.
Elisha tells the king to get a bow and arrows, and Jehoash obeys. These weapons are used as visible signs to prepare the king for the battles ahead.

Elisha directs the king to put his hands on the bow, and then the dying prophet lays his own hands on top of the king's hands. This symbolic act shows that the king's skill and military power would come entirely from the Lord.

Elisha tells the king to open the east window toward the occupied territory and shoot an arrow. As the arrow flies, Elisha declares it to be the Lord's arrow of victory, promising that Israel will defeat the Arameans at the city of Aphek.
Elisha then tells the king to take the rest of the arrows and strike the ground. Jehoash strikes the floor only three times and then abruptly stops.

Elisha is deeply grieved and angry because the king's quick stop reveals a lack of bold faith and persistence. Because Jehoash stopped after only three strikes, Israel will win only three battles instead of completely finishing off the enemy.

differ.view: The king's lack of zeal and faith was his own failure, and his half-hearted effort directly limited the victories God gave him.

notes.meaning: Elisha dies and is buried, having served God faithfully as a prophet for many decades. Sometime later, invading bands of Moabite raiders resume their seasonal plundering of Israel each spring.

While some Israelites are burying a man, they spot approaching raiders and hastily drop the body into Elisha's tomb. As soon as the dead man touches Elisha's bones, he comes back to life and stands on his feet. This miracle honors the prophet and confirms that God's power will surely bring about the national revival Elisha had promised.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some interpreters suggest the man was not truly dead but only unconscious, and the shock of the fall or the cold cave woke him up.

notes.meaning: The writer reminds the reader of how harshly King Hazael of Aram had oppressed Israel throughout the entire reign of Jehoahaz. This prolonged suffering set the stage for God's gracious rescue.

Despite Israel's long record of rebellion, the Lord shows deep compassion and refuses to wipe them out or banish them completely. He spares them because of the unbreakable covenant He made centuries earlier with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
When King Hazael of Aram dies, his son Ben-hadad III takes the throne. This change in leadership leaves the Aramean kingdom weaker, opening the way for Israel to push back.

King Jehoash defeats Ben-hadad three times in battle, exactly as Elisha had foretold with the arrows. Through these three victories, Israel takes back the towns that Aram had captured during the reign of Jehoahaz.
